glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The LORD completes the sanctuary’s furnishings with the golden altar of incense, the equal ransom paid at a census, the bronze laver for the priests’ washing, and the holy anointing oil and incense, each set apart so that Israel may approach the holy God in the way He appoints.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 30 continues the tabernacle instructions given on Sinai (chapters 25–31), following the consecration of the priests in chapter 29.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 30:1–10 — The Altar of Incense Before the Veil

  • Exodus 30:11–16 — The Ransom Money at the Census

  • Exodus 30:17–21 — The Bronze Laver for the Priests’ Washing

  • Exodus 30:22–33 — The Holy Anointing Oil

  • Exodus 30:34–38 — The Holy Incense

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And when Aaron lights the lamps at twilight, he shall burn incense on it, a perpetual incense before the LORD throughout your generations.” (Exodus 30:8)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Five instructions fill out how Israel will approach God. A small golden altar stands just before the veil, near the mercy seat, “where I will meet with you” (30:6). Every morning and every evening Aaron burns incense on it, “a perpetual incense before the LORD” (30:8). Nothing else may be offered there, and once a year even this altar is cleansed with blood. Scripture later pictures the prayers of God’s people rising like incense (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 8:3–4), and Jesus always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25).

When Israel is counted, every man pays the same half shekel as a ransom: “The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less” (30:15). Every life counts the same before God. A bronze laver stands between the altar and the tent, and the priests must wash their hands and feet before they serve, “lest they die” (30:20). Finally God gives recipes for a holy anointing oil, which consecrates the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests, and for a holy incense. Both belong to God alone and must never be copied for ordinary use. What God sets apart must stay holy.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 30:1–10 — The Altar of Incense Before the Veil

A small square altar of acacia wood covered with gold is placed before the veil, near the mercy seat where God meets with Moses. Aaron burns incense on it every morning and evening, nothing else may be offered on it, and once a year he makes atonement on its horns with blood.

Exodus 30:11–16 — The Ransom Money at the Census

Whenever Israel is counted, every man twenty years and older gives half a shekel as a ransom to the LORD, the rich no more and the poor no less, so that no plague comes on them. The money supports the service of the tabernacle as a reminder before the LORD.

Exodus 30:17–21 — The Bronze Laver for the Priests’ Washing

A bronze laver on a bronze stand is placed between the tent and the altar. Aaron and his sons must wash their hands and feet in it before entering the tent or serving at the altar, so that they will not die.

Exodus 30:22–33 — The Holy Anointing Oil

Myrrh, cinnamon, fragrant cane, cassia, and olive oil are blended into a holy anointing oil, used to consecrate the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests. It must never be copied or poured on ordinary people, because it is holy.

Exodus 30:34–38 — The Holy Incense

Stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense are blended into a salted, pure, and holy incense, and some is placed before the Testimony. No one may make it for personal use.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 30 shows that drawing near to God involves prayer, cleansing, and being set apart by Him. The incense altar stood closest to the mercy seat, a fitting picture of prayer rising before God, and of Christ who intercedes for His people. The laver pictures the cleansing Christ gives His people “with the washing of water by the word” (Ephesians 5:26), so that they can serve Him freely.

As the LORD directed, the anointing oil consecrated the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests for His service, and it was never to be used for ordinary purposes (30:26–33). Jesus is the Spirit-anointed One (Luke 4:18), and God anoints and equips His people by the same Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:21–22). The equal ransom at the census reminded Israel that no one could buy a better standing with God. Rich and poor alike owed the same price for their lives.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Incense and prayer. Incense rises morning and evening before the veil, near God’s meeting place (30:1–8).

Atonement in the holy place. Even the incense altar is cleansed once a year with blood (30:10).

Equal worth before God. Rich and poor pay the same ransom at the census (30:12–15).

Cleansing for service. The priests wash hands and feet before they serve (30:17–21).

What is holy stays holy. The anointing oil and incense are reserved for God alone (30:31–38).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Altar of incense (30:1). A small gold-covered altar in the holy place before the veil, distinct from the bronze altar of burnt offering in the courtyard.

Ransom (30:12). A payment for a life. Each man counted in a census paid half a shekel to the LORD.

Shekel of the sanctuary (30:13). The standard weight of silver used for offerings.

Laver (30:18). A bronze basin of water for the priests’ washing, placed between the tent and the altar.

Anointing oil (30:25). A fragrant oil made by a set recipe and used only to consecrate the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests.

focus: Exodus 30 completes the sanctuary’s furnishings and supplies with five separate instructions from the LORD: the golden altar of incense, the ransom money paid at a census, the bronze laver for the priests’ washing, the holy anointing oil, and the holy incense. Each provision has its own purpose in keeping Israel’s approach to the holy God ordered and set apart.

sections.title: The Altar of Incense Before the Veil
sections.summary: A small square altar of acacia wood overlaid with gold is placed before the veil, near the mercy seat “where I will meet with you” (Exodus 30:6). Aaron burns incense on it every morning and evening, no other offering is made on it, and once a year he makes atonement on its horns with blood.

sections.title: The Ransom Money at the Census
sections.summary: When Israel is numbered, every man twenty years old and above gives half a shekel as a ransom to the LORD, the rich no more and the poor no less, so that no plague will come among them. The atonement money is used for the service of the tabernacle of meeting as a memorial before the LORD.

sections.title: The Bronze Laver for the Priests’ Washing
sections.summary: A bronze laver with a bronze base stands between the tabernacle of meeting and the altar. Aaron and his sons must wash their hands and feet in it before they enter the tent or serve at the altar, “lest they die” (Exodus 30:20).

sections.title: The Holy Anointing Oil
sections.summary: Myrrh, cinnamon, fragrant cane, cassia, and olive oil are blended into a holy anointing oil, which is used to consecrate the tabernacle, its furnishings, and Aaron and his sons as priests. It must never be copied or used on ordinary people, for “It is holy, and it shall be holy to you” (Exodus 30:32).

sections.title: The Holy Incense
sections.summary: Stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense are blended into an incense that is “salted, pure, and holy” (Exodus 30:35), and some is placed before the Testimony. No one may make it for personal use.

1.brief: Israel is to make an altar of acacia wood to burn incense on. A second altar is added for the holy place.
1.explain:
“You shall make an altar to burn incense on; you shall make it of acacia wood.”

A second altar is added, not for animal sacrifice but “to burn incense.” It is distinct from the bronze altar in the courtyard (27:1–8).

2.brief: The altar is square, a cubit long and wide and two cubits high, with horns of one piece with it. The incense altar is small but shaped like the great altar.
2.explain:
“A cubit shall be its length and a cubit its width—it shall be square—and two cubits shall be its height.”

The incense altar is small, about 18 inches square and 3 feet high.

“Its horns shall be of one piece with it.”

Like the great altar, it has “horns.” The incense altar is small but shaped like the altar of burnt offering.

3.brief: Its top, sides, and horns are overlaid with pure gold, with a gold molding around it. It belongs with the gold furnishings of the holy place.
3.explain:
“And you shall overlay its top, its sides all around, and its horns with pure gold;”

It is covered with “pure gold,” unlike the bronze altar outside.

“and you shall make for it a molding of gold all around.”

A gold “molding” frames the top. It belongs with the gold furnishings of the holy place.

4.brief: Two gold rings are made under the molding on both sides to hold the poles. It is made to travel.
4.explain:
“Two gold rings you shall make for it, under the molding on both its sides.”

Two gold rings are attached under the molding.

“You shall place them on its two sides, and they will be holders for the poles with which to bear it.”

The rings hold the carrying poles. It is made to travel.

5.brief: The poles are made of acacia wood and overlaid with gold. Its carrying poles match the other gold furniture.
5.explain:
“You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold.”

The poles match the other gold furniture.

6.brief: The altar is placed before the veil, in front of the mercy seat, “where I will meet with you.” The incense altar stands close to the place of God’s meeting.
6.explain:
“And you shall put it before the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony,”

The altar stands in the holy place, directly “before the veil.”

“before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony, where I will meet with you.”

On the other side of the veil is “the mercy seat,” “where I will meet with you.” The incense altar stands as close as possible to the place of God’s meeting.
6.notes: Hebrews 9:3–4 associates the golden censer, or altar of incense, with the Most Holy Place, probably because of its close link with the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12–13, 18).

7.brief: Aaron is to burn sweet incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps. Incense rises before God at the start of each day.
7.explain:
“Aaron shall burn on it sweet incense every morning;”

Aaron burns “sweet incense every morning.”

“when he tends the lamps, he shall burn incense on it.”

The incense is burned when the lamps are tended. Incense rises before God at the start of each day.
7.notes: Zacharias was burning incense in the temple when the angel Gabriel appeared to him, while “the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense” (Luke 1:8–10).

8.brief: When Aaron lights the lamps at twilight, he burns incense, “a perpetual incense before the LORD.” The incense rises continually, morning and evening.
8.explain:
“And when Aaron lights the lamps at twilight, he shall burn incense on it,”

Incense is burned again in the evening.

“a perpetual incense before the LORD throughout your generations.”

It is “a perpetual incense,” rising morning and evening without fail. The incense rises continually before God. The incense pictures prayer. David prayed, “Let my prayer be set before You as incense,” linking it with the evening sacrifice (Psalm 141:2), and Revelation 5:8 describes “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” Christ “always lives to make intercession” for His people (Hebrews 7:25).

9.brief: No strange incense, burnt offering, grain offering, or drink offering may be offered on it. The altar is reserved for the incense God appoints, and Scripture later pictures the prayers of God’s people as incense.
9.explain:
“You shall not offer strange incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering;”

No “strange incense,” incense not made by God’s recipe (30:34–38), may be offered. No animal or grain offerings may be burned on it.

“nor shall you pour a drink offering on it.”

The altar is reserved for the incense God appoints. Nadab and Abihu died when they offered “profane fire” that God had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1–2).

10.brief: Once a year Aaron makes atonement on its horns with the blood of the sin offering, “It is most holy to the LORD.” Even the altar of incense needs yearly cleansing by blood.
10.explain:
“And Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonement;”

“Once a year,” on the Day of Atonement, Aaron puts blood on the horns of this altar (Leviticus 16:18–19). This yearly blood rite is distinct from the daily burning of incense.

“once a year he shall make atonement upon it throughout your generations. It is most holy to the LORD.”

Even the altar of incense needs yearly cleansing by blood.

11.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses again. A new instruction concerns the people themselves.
11.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:”

A new instruction concerns the people themselves.

12.brief: When Israel is counted, every man must give a ransom for himself to the LORD so that no plague comes on them. The census is a solemn act before God.
12.explain:
“When you take the census of the children of Israel for their number,”

When Israel is counted, a special offering is required.

“then every man shall give a ransom for himself to the LORD, when you number them, that there may be no plague among them when you number them.”

Each man counted must give “a ransom for himself,” a price paid for his life. Counting the people was a solemn act. They belonged to God, and the ransom acknowledged that. The payment was given “that there may be no plague.”
12.notes: In 2 Samuel 24 David took a census of Israel, and a plague followed (2 Samuel 24:1–15). That account does not mention this ransom or say that it went unpaid.

13.brief: Each person counted gives half a shekel by the sanctuary shekel as an offering to the LORD. Every man gives the same amount.
13.explain:
“This is what everyone among those who are numbered shall give: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (a shekel is twenty gerahs).”

The amount is “half a shekel,” measured by the standard “shekel of the sanctuary.” A shekel was a weight of silver, about two-fifths of an ounce.

“The half-shekel shall be an offering to the LORD.”

The payment is “an offering to the LORD.” Every man gives the same amount.
13.notes: In Jesus’ day this was collected as the temple tax. Jesus provided the coin for Himself and Peter from a fish’s mouth (Matthew 17:24–27).

14.brief: Everyone twenty years old and above who is counted gives the offering. The ransom applies to all adult men.
14.explain:
“Everyone included among those who are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering to the LORD.”

All counted men “from twenty years old and above” must give. Twenty was the age for military service (Numbers 1:3).

15.brief: The rich must not give more and the poor must not give less than half a shekel, “to make atonement for yourselves.” Every life is of equal worth before God.
15.explain:
“The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel,”

Everyone pays exactly the same. “The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less.” Every life is of equal worth before God.

“when you give an offering to the LORD, to make atonement for yourselves.”

The payment is “to make atonement,” to cover or ransom their lives.

16.brief: The atonement money is used for the service of the tabernacle as a memorial before the LORD. The ransom supports God’s dwelling and reminds Israel of their need.
16.explain:
“And you shall take the atonement money of the children of Israel, and shall appoint it for the service of the tabernacle of meeting,”

The ransom silver is used “for the service of the tabernacle.” Exodus 38:25–28 records that it made the silver sockets and hooks.

“that it may be a memorial for the children of Israel before the LORD, to make atonement for yourselves.”

It is “a memorial” before God. The ransom supports God’s dwelling and reminds Israel of their need.

17.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses again. The next instruction concerns washing.
17.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:”

The next instruction concerns washing.

18.brief: A bronze laver with a bronze base is made for washing and placed between the tabernacle and the altar, filled with water. The laver stands on the way into God’s presence.
18.explain:
“You shall also make a laver of bronze, with its base also of bronze, for washing.”

“A laver of bronze,” a large basin, is made “for washing.” Exodus 38:8 says it was made from the bronze mirrors of the women who served at the tent’s door.

“You shall put it between the tabernacle of meeting and the altar. And you shall put water in it,”

It stands “between the tabernacle of meeting and the altar.” A priest passed the altar and then the laver before entering the tent. The laver stands on the way into God’s presence.

19.brief: Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet in it. The priests must be cleansed for their work.
19.explain:
“for Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet in water from it.”

The priests wash “their hands and their feet.” Hands did the work. Feet walked in the holy place. The priests must be cleansed for their work.

20.brief: The priests must wash when they enter the tabernacle or approach the altar to minister, “lest they die.” Cleansing is required before serving God.
20.explain:
“When they go into the tabernacle of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to the LORD,”

They must wash every time they enter the tent or serve at the altar.

“they shall wash with water, lest they die.”

Neglecting this washing brings death. Cleansing is required before serving God.

21.brief: The priests must wash their hands and feet “lest they die,” as a statute forever for Aaron and his descendants. The repeated warning stresses how seriously God takes it.
21.explain:
“So they shall wash their hands and their feet, lest they die.”

The warning “lest they die” is repeated. God takes this washing very seriously.

“And it shall be a statute forever to them—to him and his descendants throughout their generations.”

It is a permanent rule for Aaron’s line. The washing at the laver pictures the cleansing Christ gives His people. Paul writes that Christ gave Himself for the church “that He might sanctify and cleanse her with the washing of water by the word” (Ephesians 5:25–26), and Hebrews 10:22 speaks of “our bodies washed with pure water.” This washing has its own purpose, distinct from the census ransom and from the sacrifices.

22.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses. The next instruction concerns the anointing oil.
22.explain:
“Moreover the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:”

The next instruction concerns the anointing oil.

23.brief: Moses is to take fine spices: liquid myrrh, sweet-smelling cinnamon, and sweet-smelling cane in fixed amounts. The oil is made from costly ingredients.
23.explain:
“Also take for yourself quality spices—five hundred shekels of liquid myrrh,”

The oil begins with “liquid myrrh,” a fragrant resin.

“half as much sweet-smelling cinnamon (two hundred and fifty shekels), two hundred and fifty shekels of sweet-smelling cane,”

“Cinnamon” and “sweet-smelling cane” are added in fixed amounts. The oil is made from costly ingredients.

24.brief: Cassia and a hin of olive oil complete the ingredients, measured by the sanctuary shekel. The recipe is precise.
24.explain:
“five hundred shekels of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, and a hin of olive oil.”

“Cassia,” a bark like cinnamon, and “a hin of olive oil” complete the recipe. The proportions are precise.
24.notes: The spices together weighed about 37 pounds, blended into about a gallon of oil. The quantities are approximate, since the weight of the sanctuary shekel and the size of a hin are not known exactly.

25.brief: The spices and oil are made into a holy anointing oil, blended by the art of the perfumer. The oil is set apart for holy use.
25.explain:
“And you shall make from these a holy anointing oil, an ointment compounded according to the art of the perfumer.”

The ingredients are blended by “the art of the perfumer.”

“It shall be a holy anointing oil.”

The result is “a holy anointing oil,” set apart for God’s use alone.

26.brief: The oil is used to anoint the tabernacle and the ark of the Testimony. Anointing begins with God’s dwelling.
26.explain:
“With it you shall anoint the tabernacle of meeting and the ark of the Testimony;”

The anointing begins with “the tabernacle” and “the ark.”

27.brief: The table and its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, and the incense altar are also anointed. Every furnishing of the holy place is set apart.
27.explain:
“the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar of incense;”

Every furnishing of the holy place is anointed.

28.brief: The altar of burnt offering and its utensils and the laver and its base are anointed. The courtyard furnishings are included.
28.explain:
“the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the laver and its base.”

The courtyard furnishings are anointed too.

29.brief: Moses consecrates them so they are most holy, and “whatever touches them must be holy.” The anointing makes everything belong to God.
29.explain:
“You shall consecrate them, that they may be most holy;”

The anointing makes them “most holy.”

“whatever touches them must be holy.”

As with the altar (29:37), anything that touches them must itself be holy. The anointing makes everything belong to God.

30.brief: Moses is to anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them as priests. The same oil sets apart the priests and the sanctuary.
30.explain:
“And you shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may minister to Me as priests.”

The same oil that sets apart the sanctuary sets apart the priests (29:7, 21).

31.brief: Israel is told that this is “a holy anointing oil to Me throughout your generations.” The oil belongs to God for all time.
31.explain:
“And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: ‘This shall be a holy anointing oil to Me throughout your generations.”

The oil belongs to God “throughout your generations.”

32.brief: The oil may not be poured on ordinary people or copied in its composition, “It is holy, and it shall be holy to you.” What God sets apart must not be treated as common.
32.explain:
“It shall not be poured on man’s flesh; nor shall you make any other like it, according to its composition.”

It may not be used on ordinary people or copied.

“It is holy, and it shall be holy to you.”

What God sets apart must not be treated as common. The anointing oil points to the Holy Spirit, who anoints Christ and His people for service. Jesus read, “The Spirit of the LORD is upon Me,” and said the Spirit had anointed Him (Luke 4:18). Paul writes that God “has anointed us” and “given us the Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee” (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).

33.brief: Whoever makes oil like it or puts it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people. Misusing the holy oil is a grave offense.
33.explain:
“Whoever compounds any like it, or whoever puts any of it on an outsider, shall be cut off from his people.”

Making a copy or using it on “an outsider” brings the penalty of being “cut off.” Misusing the holy oil is a grave offense.

34.brief: The LORD tells Moses to take sweet spices, stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, in equal amounts. The incense also has a fixed recipe.
34.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses: ‘Take sweet spices, stacte and onycha and galbanum, and pure frankincense with these sweet spices;”

The incense has its own recipe of four ingredients. “Frankincense” was a white resin with a strong fragrance. The other three are uncertain substances, perhaps resins and shell extracts.

“there shall be equal amounts of each.”

The four are blended in equal measure.

35.brief: The spices are made into incense, blended by the perfumer, “salted, pure, and holy.” The incense is set apart for God.
35.explain:
“You shall make of these an incense, a compound according to the art of the perfumer, salted, pure, and holy.”

The incense is “salted, pure, and holy.” Salt was added to all offerings (Leviticus 2:13). The incense is set apart for God.

36.brief: Some is beaten very fine and placed before the Testimony “where I will meet with you,” and it is most holy. The incense is offered near God’s meeting place.
36.explain:
“And you shall beat some of it very fine, and put some of it before the Testimony in the tabernacle of meeting where I will meet with you.”

Some is ground “very fine” and placed “before the Testimony,” near God’s meeting place.

“It shall be most holy to you.”

The incense is “most holy.”

37.brief: Israel must not make any for themselves by the same recipe, for it is holy for the LORD. The incense is reserved for God alone.
37.explain:
“But as for the incense which you shall make, you shall not make any for yourselves, according to its composition.”

Israel must not make it for personal use.

“It shall be to you holy for the LORD.”

The incense is reserved for God alone.

38.brief: Whoever makes anything like it to enjoy its smell shall be cut off from his people. The holy incense may never be used for personal pleasure.
38.explain:
“Whoever makes any like it, to smell it, he shall be cut off from his people.”

Anyone who makes it “to smell it,” for personal enjoyment, is cut off. The holy incense may never be used for personal pleasure.
